projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert J. Turner was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Robert J. Turner. Mr. Turner served in the U.S. Coast Guard onboard the Patrol Frigate USS Racine PF100. He served in the Atlantic, Pacific, and Mediterranean theaters. At his highest rank was Water Tender at Second Class. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded on January 21, 2005 at Mr. Turner's home in Eastlake, Ohio. Bob was 84 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: _____+ living at 143rd Street in Cleveland, Ohio. It was my parents' home. (Calwood)-- North (?Calwood?) on lakeshore Boulevard.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You told me-- let's see-- you're 84 now?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So that would mean you were about-- what--

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: 20 years old.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: --20 years old?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: 20 years old-- 21-- 21. I worked at White Motors-- White Motors Company as a welder. After I got out of high school I worked at an Army half track store. And when the draft come-- I missed the first draft-- I didn't get drafted so I went-- the second draft I registered for the draft and when the notice had come out there was a building in (Calwood) that called the scoop that made a little newspaper. And they put all the kids' names on the windows up there and I stopped to look for my name and I thought my God I missed the draft. They're not going to get me. But a week later I got a letter from East Cleveland-- they moved me up to East Cleveland because there's no kids up there. East Cleveland's not like it is now. Oh, that was a beautiful town in it's day-- you know when the-- nothing like it is now. Well, then-- so then I went downtown-- I went down to the Keys Building and I enlisted on the sixth of July, 1942.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Before that do you have specific memories of the attack on Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Oh yeah, yeah. Yeah. I was driving-- my brother and I were coming out-- we'd had a-- we kids-- we lived out here. This is where I live now was all the summer cottages, and up here behind the harbor bar was a ball field. Right over here on Lakewood Boulevard and we had quite a ball team. One time in 1937, we won-- took everything in lake-- lake championships. We come out here in the summertime--there was a lot of-- had a hell of a ball team. And that day at Pearl Harbor attack my brother and I were driving out-- I had a-- I had about a 1934 Chevy-- I had it-- was driving and got to about Council Bend-- you know where that is?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I think I do, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: They--they tore the building down-- that was Council Bend. And the-- announced over the radio that-- that the Japs attacked Pearl Harbor. That was around noon. We're heading out here for a party for the-- the ____ were putting on a baseball party for us kids. Well, a year later every kid was gone. All the kids that played ball together, you know, were all gone.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What did you think when you heard that news on the radio?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Nothing. Just that-- well, I heard that he-- you know-- Roosevelt put an embargo on the coal of the Japs and there could be something coming up about that, but I didn't hear much. In them days you didn't get the news like you get it now. You want the news you go to the picture show and get the RKO or the press would have it. Something pressed in the-- then the-- at that time they had the Cleveland News. {coughs} They had three newspapers that's in the town then.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So then you were called in July of '42?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: No, I enlisted July of '42 and I was called up the seventh of August. I was sworn in.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Seventh of August downtown Cleveland. And I was down-- my dad took me downtown and hung around down there 'til about four or five o'clock then they put us on a train. Then they swore us in, put us on a train and at midnight I wound up in Buffalo, New York. That's supposed to be the boot camp but it was no boot camp. And they put us-- they took us down to the Buffalo base right there at the mouth of the Black River-- at the Black Rock or Black River there-- and they have the Coast Guard stationed and they had an old boat tied up there what they called the _____. It was an old passenger ship from-- sailed the lakes-- it was, oh it was an old one. Well, they get in there at midnight and I thought by God I've got to go to sea already. Well anyhow they put us on this old tub and it was a very small state-- it was two little bunks and a small state and under each boat was--was a pee pot. Spent the night-- they gave us two blankets and a pillow-- no pillow cover or nothing, no case like that and-- I spent the night on the boat and the next morning for breakfast I went up to-- they had to give us breakfast. I remember it was a little-- little half a bowl of oatmeal and a half a pint of chocolate milk to put on top it. That was our breakfast. Well then-- laid around there in Buffalo-- then they-- at that time they were bringing the city of Buffalo in. They were going to make ___ out of it the airplane carrier for the lakes. Well we had to go to stand fire watch in that at night. Nothing to eat and I remember one night we were over there standing fire watch and-- and we found a barrel of pickles-- or a bottle of olives down in the-- in the galley. It was half-- almost empty. We got-- ate a few olives. Then one time they made us put our white uniforms on and go fight the fire over the dump in Buffalo. Last time I drove by there was a housing development. It was all condos.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Why did you pick the Coast Guard? Why'd you enlist in the Coast Guard?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Well, I lived out here in the harbor and at the time there was a lot of fellows out here that were into Coast Guard. The auxiliary out here in Fairport. Then the second thing it was I didn't want to go out a big ship because it was too many men on it. They have a thousand men-- I didn't want to be on a big ship I want something small. And I was up at the bank one time up in Cleveland-- Cleveland Trust in Willoughby on-- and I come out of the bank they had a big poster out there of a Coast Guard ship, a 84, a little small 84 footer with a guy on the front bow with a machine gun. I thought boy, that's for me. That so-- that's why I enlisted. And that-- the second thing too-- the Coast Guard then you had to have all your teeth and a high school education. It was a little different then the Navy. And I went down there-- when I enlisted they said teeth are crooked. He said-- you might have to get a waiver. I said hell, I'll go down and join the Navy then. He says oh, never mind we'll waive it. So, that's-- they let me in then. Well then, played around in Buffalo-- God-- but they-- there was no organization. Because those kids were coming in from all over the ninth neighborhood district: Detroit, South Europe, all over, all at once. Pouring in. And they had nothing for us to do. So then they shipped us to Erie. And they took us up there to-- in a truck. And we went to the rifle range and played around there for a day or two then they took us back and we stayed at the Black Rock-- Black Rock Canal right underneath the-- underneath the Peace Bridge. It was a-- the Buffalo Yacht Club had a building there. We stayed in that building. Well then they shipped me, I went to-- got-- wound up in Ashtabula. Coast Guard station there, well my job was-- there was the morning I got up and put the water the-- there was a three gallon milk can, my job was to add water to it so everybody'd have enough. Then there was and I and R boat come in and they wanted somebody to go on that boat so hell I jumped on it. It was in Negani, an old I and R boat, 300-foot long. Sailed for Cleveland Cliffs. Well I got on that-- they made another kid-- he was from Berea-- well no, he was from around-- yeah, Berea I think it was. Down around there was a-- his folks had a dairy farm and he was the-- and him and I were on that boat together. We sailed-- then the next-- we sailed from here all up to ______+ and Escanaba up to-- well, up to the Sioux Canal. And then I got on another one, the Corvus. That was, I think it was a Mather Ship-- armed guard we were supposed to-- two of us--

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So they had regular Coast Guard armed guards on the--

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Yeah, every officer on the ship was a commissioned officer. And the-- two of us were armed guards. They had a 30/30 rifle. The damn barrel was bent was full of dirt you couldn't see through it, no bullets. I don't know what the hell we were supposed to do. Supposed to stand watch it was restricted water ways. Well, I stayed on that one until Thanksgiving Day it was in Lake Ohana docks in 1942, Buffalo. It was so rough we couldn't go out. So we had--we stayed there for Thanksgiving-- had a beautiful Thanksgiving dinner off that-- had ducks, geese, had everything. The way they fed them I and R boats was the best feeder got the best crews. If you've got a reputation of a bad feeder nobody wanted to sail on that day. Them days there was about 300 I and R boats and I remember one time being in one in them up in-- up in White Fish Bay and I counted 54 I and R boats in anchored-- that's where the-- where Fitzgerald went down. Right there on the other side of the Sioux. Well, I stayed on that until that winter I got off-- they took me off in Toledo and I hung around up there and captain of the port. He had a-- they-- they a Jeep-- they got a Jeep up there and they had us go around at night. It was funny, the first Jeep they got would-- the fellows would ride around to all these I and R boats they're all laid up there in the basin and it was an officer and a chief and the officer to ride around in that Jeep. And then he got sick of that so that it was-- it was a chief and a first class man and a petty officer. And it winds up two seamen doing the job-- two second class seaman because it was goddamn cold. Boy, it was a cold winter. Well, I did that-- oh, and before that I wound up in the hospital-- I had pneumonia, I fell in the river-- the river-- got pneumonia. I laid in the hospital 14 days with a _____ blanket on me. That's why I found out I couldn't take Penicillin. And-- that sulfa drug make me start itching here. Well then I went back to the station and I heard there was an opening coming up on the lighthouse out there in Toledo. Toledo Harbor Light-- it was nine-- 10 miles out on the lake. It was off of Monroe, Michigan. So I went out there. The commander was a guy named Herman Barr and the two other fellows John-- oh, one from was Saginaw, Michigan one was from New York. There was four of us out there. I was the only one with a high school education. 10 miles out on the lake and every four weeks together we get five days off. You worked out there seven days a week and every night you go out and watch the-- you go up and wind the light up. The light was up-- how many feet up-- 60 so, three decks up and you had to go up there at night and every turn to wind up it had a box with a cable in it and you wind it up and that cable would drop and as it dropped the light would turn. And it was a beautiful light, it was made in France. We weren't allowed to touch it. The keeper was the only one that could wipe it off-- he had a ____ you know. Well I stayed out there until fall then I took an aptitude test. A Yeoman come out and I took an aptitude test and that winter I went into-- I went into the base and I got a call in the-- to the office-- the Lieutenant wanted to see me. And he says you're going to go to school in New York City, Water Tender school. And I said I'll have to go to ask my father. I said I can't do that. So-- so in the meantime when I was standing guard up there-- in Toledo there-- there was, about three or four big refineries there you know, that was a hell of a refinery town. There was a boat and they were loading oil and I was standing there talking to the captain. A little old guy there was getting ready to retire, it was the Cleveco. You hear about the Cleveco?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: The Cleveco was a tanker and it had a tug-- the admiral--the wooden tug-- it was a wooden tug. It was 80 foot long, it was painted gray and the Cleveco was a barge. And this-- were loading oil. Well they come down here-- up there right about Christmas day of 1942 when I was going back and I was off at White City 140th Street at Lakeshore Boulevard. I heard a whistle-- it was snowing like hell-- Cleveco was-- the tug sunk off of an awful rain. And the Cleveco had drifted and it sunk, right about off of _____. It was quite a thing in it's day-- a full load of oil and all the crew were lost. I was talking to that ol' captain he was a guy standing with old-- old overcoat on you know-- and he was going to retire. Well then, they shipped me to New York City. I left, it was me and another kid. We left by train and got to-- went up to-- got onto Broadway. We had to go find the Coast Guard station. They shipped us over to the Hotel Sutton down on Second Avenue and 48th in New York. And we went to school in the _____+. It was right underneath the Brooklyn Bridge. It was going to be a water tendered, boiler room. So I went to school and lived in the-- lived in the hotel. We did real good. I got good grades-- I got my rate. But when the rates came out-- used to come out the second class so ours were the first class come out as a third. I was so god damn mad, wanted to get in second but came out third so-- then they shipped me to Norfolk, Virginia. And on Naval operating base and got assigned to a ship-- the United States ship Racine. Then I went to Manhattan Beach and laid around there waiting for the ship. The ship was here being built in Cleveland down behind the stadium. And it was-- there was-- they built 75 of them all over the country. Well this-- then they put Coast Guard crews on them-- it was a Navy ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: And what kind of ship was it again?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: It's what they call a Patrol Frigate. It was about 300-foot long and-- excuse me-- and on October--that-- of '44 they shipped us up to South Chicago-- its South Chicago-- we went on the builders trial out in the-- off of Milwaukee. And they accepted the ship and the guys in the boiler room-- that had a civilian down there. They said okay boys, it's all yours. So me and my buddy spent all night picking up floor plates tracing lines, oil lines, water lines. You know-- what the hell we get-- and the boilers were three decks higher-- what they call a water tube boiler express type. On the I and R boats they had what they call a scotch boilers. They were tubes in water--it was around the tubes. On an express type boat the water was in the tubes and the fire outside of it. It was two decks higher with a blower on top and he had a--a very small room. It was only about half as big as this kitchen--you know--and the water pumps and--Christ--all kinds of stuff. And we had two reciprocating engines-- what they call three (leggers)-- a steam engine, if you know. Then I--we picked up a ship in South Chicago and it went on to builders trial and they accepted it and we left from there to Joliet, Illinois. We went down to Kalkan to Joliet, Illinois and they jacked up the ship. They put tanks in with screws and we started out the Mississippi river. It took 30 something days going down the Mississippi and we're allowed-- we're not off the ship. But every morning the deck was full of mud.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How'd that happen?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Yeah, because we tied up every night. We got 30 days down to New Orleans and then they cut us loose and we went across the bay over to Galveston, Houston. And they took us off the ship and put us into-- they had to do some more work on it-- they took the crew into Galveston--Fort Crockett-- it was a big Army base. It was a Naval Annex and I got a job there to drive a Navy bus. My job was to go out at midnight and go down to the police station and pick up all the drunks and bring them back. The big school bus. I did that, then we shipped out of there and went into commission on January of '45. They put us into commission-- we started out-- there and we down the builders-- sea trials and we went to-- we went to Bermuda. Yeah, they took-- we went to Bermuda. And then from Bermuda we picked up-- we anchored out at Hamilton Bay. And you could see the (series) And the horses and all that but enlisted men were allowed no liberty. They didn't want us to go ashore there. We weren't allowed ashore but the officers went ashore. And we weren't allowed cameras. Enlisted got no cameras but the officers go to shore and they had movie cameras and they had golf clubs. And we had--we weren't allowed off the ship. We laid around there, then we went down to monkey around on exercises for a while and then we took-- picked up an Italian submarine, a mine layer. And took the crew out of our ship and took the miner. We went to Cuba with it. Took it down to Cuba. On the way down off of Florida we picked up what they thought was a submarine. They dropped a few bombs but nothing happened. They get over it-- oh, just leave it alone and keep on your course. Then we come back and we stopped in a place like Norfolk, Boston, New York City. When we got off in New York City we got orders and went out and joined a convoy off of New York City. We were supposed to be going over to France but we wound up in Mers-el-Kebir, North Africa-- Iran. And you couldn't make drinking water out of there because there was-- they were all bombed out. The _____ French-- Churchill ordered that Navy to come back over to England and join them or get bombed out. Well, they didn't do it so they bombed out and they destroyed-- knocked all the hell-- well, the battleship sunk, there was bodies on it. The water was polluted, you couldn't make-- you couldn't use converters to make salt water you know, it turns to steam and condense it. {cough} Well, we had to take the was salted up that's why put it in and when the boilers salt up its like beer foam in a glass, you can't read it. You got two water gauges. You've got to read second deck up there and-- just a three drum boiler. Two drums here and one on top and then the middle deck-- the fire deck was on the way with three burners you had to control. Every time they changed speed you had to change your burners. Carried 250 pounds of steam pressure all the time. Would stop we're wide open, you know. Its 250 pounds.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When did you make that cross into North Africa?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When did you make that cross into North Africa?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: In May.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: May of '45?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Roosevelt-- I guess he just-- he was over there then, too, or something. That was just before the war ended.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I guessed you--Roosevelt died in April --

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Yeah, I remember we were coming back-- we were coming back from over there and we was off Azores. I was up on deck sunning myself-- it was May-- and they made an announcement on the PA that Roosevelt passed away. Then we came into Portland, Maine-- Casco Bay-- we laid around there, oh, I don't know about a month maybe or a couple weeks I guess and of course Casco Bay was quite a good port for liberty. Well then they took us--

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Get in any trouble?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: No, I never did. I never got in any trouble. There was a-- the women up there were all wild up there, it was quite a-- quite a town. We'd hang around-- go up to the-- the hotel. The Falmouth Hotel in Casco Bay. Well then-- then they took us into-- sent us into New York. Went up to one of the-- they had a place out there, I forget the-- Tompkinsville-- I think it was. They put us under big sheds. And they would-- we had to pump the oil out because they were going to reinforce the rivers. They were supposed to go to Alaska. They got to pump the rivers-- they had about five of us on the ship. Nothing to eat, no place to sleep. It was a goddamn mess, no heat. So we did that and-- that's my wife.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Hi.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: We did-- we laid around there-- and supposed to reinforce-- pump oil out, steam clean the tanks and the-- put new (ribs) in that. We were going to go to Alaska. So then we started out-- we left there and I remember they called me up on deck on the seventh of August to give me my good conduct medal, three years of 4.0. I got the metal, and got into-- got into Panama and they dropped the bomb just about that time. They dropped the bomb and we was so-- I remember getting up on deck and seeing that sign that says Cologne. I thought they're selling perfume down here, is that the name of the town-- Cologne?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: We went to-- the next day went to Panama City and that's when the war was over. I thought hell, I'm going to go home now, go up here-- go to California. Instead we went out to Pearl Harbor, out to the Hawaiian Islands. Stayed out there for three days and then from there we went out to the Philippines. And we stayed out in the Philippines and hit about every island out there. We was out there for nine months. We was supposed to be in the invasion of Japan which was going to be November but it never came up. But we, the kept us out. They froze my rate. And I couldn't get out-- they didn't have-- I had-- you needed 33 points to get out and I only had 23 because I had no dependents so I lost ten points. So they froze my rate and I stayed out there so, then we come back. How did we got back-- we got back to the states-- it was at the South China Sea-- oh Christ-- we worked all through-- I remember Christmas morning of 1945 I come up on deck, I come off a watch at four o'clock in the morning I went up on deck and we were heading for Subic Bay. And-- and they made an announcement over the PA we are now passing Fort _____...(2 seconds). We just-- four o'clock in the morning-- the light, just looked like something out of a Disney Movie. {cough} We pulled into Subic Bay, they were going to-- need a new generator on the right side. I got into Subic Bay and there's no liberty. The _____ was 40 miles away, no liberty. And no mail. The post office was closed off for three days. Hell we'd been out at sea 35, 40 days. We'd go out for 45, 50 days at a time. And the sister ship, the old passing boat they just relieved us they got in a typhoon. And they were out lost for five days, they give them up. Well anyhow, stayed out there then we--

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What did they have you do when you were going around to the different islands there?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Oh we'd just anchored out. You didn't do anything, go-- there's no place to go.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: They just had you-- you were just going from island to island?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Just come out-- be out on the sea 300 miles out. And then we'd come in like been to South China Sea, ____, ____ all of Gulf-- all through there and then lay-- we'd lay-- there's nothing out there. There's no food. We didn't have nothing to eat for Christ-- we were starving to death out there.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was the purpose of doing all this?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Air sea rescue. The ships were coming home-- airplanes they-- they'd pick up the signal.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Oh, just in case there was a problem?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Yeah, they'd pick up the signals. Watch out for them. And we had-- it was a weather ship. We had ____+ on there. We, the-- this ship wasn't made for, for any kind of fight. They had depth charge, they had a submarine was about all they could do. There is nothing you couldn't do. It had two little 300 guns on it, two 20 millimeter aircraft, but they-- no armor on the damn thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: But you never called on any rescue missions or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: No, a lot of the stuff in the enlisted men-- you know-- there's a lot of discrimination in the service. You got the top man. Well he-- we had a guy, it was a man--Commander ____. He was an academy man, he was a pilot. And he got grounded because he-- well, now that's what I heard-- he drove a-- he flew a PBY under a bridge so they grounded him. They made him captain of the ship was on. He was a nut. And then they shipped 17 months and never talked to him.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Oh really?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: You'd never see an officer up on deck at night after dark. Yeah, I'd go roam around-- that's when I don't like being on a small ship we'd have to go up to the pilot house and-- but it was my buddies up there and then I'd go down like at night I'd go in the engineer's office and use his typewriter and write a letter home.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How many men were on that ship?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: About 300.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: 300. It was-- you ever read Mr. Roberts?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: This is about the same type of ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Okay. All right.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Don't know where the hell we're going or what we're doing, just doing it. Well I think I'd end up-- start home in May and stopped at Pearl Harbor for three days, then we come in to Seattle on the 12th of May, Mother's Day. I'll never forget that. 12th of May and I got--got off the ship and the captain and the crew were standing up there on the deck and everybody said goodbye to us. Been with the guys 17 months, never said goodbye. Went into Seattle and played around there about three days. Processed us out and then we went to Detroit. Detroit was the head of the Ninth Naval District. I stayed in there for three days. I got called in one of the lieutenant's office in he says you, you owe 75 dollars income taxes from 1941. I says I'm not going to pay it. I says Goddamn it I just give you three years of my life I'm not paying it. He says you got a terrible attitude. 75 bucks. When I got out, got my discharge I started home and the railroad went on strike so I had to walk from-- hitchhike from Detroit to Toledo. My dad my mother and my wife picked me up, brought me home. But that was it, it was three years and nine months.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was that reunion with your family like when you got back?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Well, I just met my dad and mother and Pat up in-- up at Toledo, in front of-- you ever been to Toledo?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah, sure.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: They got the Toledo Blade, the newspaper.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Well, I was there in front of the bus station, they met me at the station and it was a woman reporter, she wanted me to take my picture taking-- buying a ticket, you know. And it's-- funny thing was, her husband was the executive officer on the ship was on. He was from Toledo. Then I saw Pat and my mother thought I left-- got into see-- go-- come home, you know. That was--

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Any-- any parties or anything?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: No. No. No. No, the war was over nine months when I got home.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I guess that's true. Yeah been over for--

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: It wasn't-- it was-- I don't know. There's nothing like it is now. You didn't have the news, you didn't have-- you didn't have no refrigeration. You had no TV, you didn't have anything you got now.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Gratefully, you still had buttons and your pants you know what I mean-- see-- it's all the difference in the world. And the food was altogether different.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was their reaction when the guys heard that news when they dropped the atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Just-- yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Nothing. Nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Just, you knew it was inevitable--

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: No, you didn't know what's going to happen. You didn't know anything about that kind of stuff. You know, we never get no news.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Couldn't even understand what an atomic bomb was--

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: No, the only time-- the only time you hear something was when somebody would be up on the bridge with the captain and hear the officers talking. You know-- we didn't know what the hell was going on. They didn't tell us nothing. I had friends in radio they'd come by and give you a scoop sheet once in a while, other than that you didn't know what the hell was going on. It's not like it is now. You didn't have that-- you didn't have these little radios or anything like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Well, you said you were at sea for long periods of time what'd--

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Yeah, 35, 40 days.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: --what'd you'd do to-- what'd you do to pass the time when you were--

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Go sit on the ____ rack and bull shit.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: We had no place to sit down. You'll see them sit down one of those stantions or you go sit on the ____ rack. There-- there was no-- if you want to sit down you go down the mass deck they had a little-- couple little benches down there. Sit on a bench. They didn't take care-- no-- nothing to eat. Christ, you had no food. Every time you come into a port we never-- the food ship left two days ago or something. You just-- never no fresh food. One night the officers got some--some potatoes and they were frying them up there. Holy Christ you could smell them all over the ship. My mouth was watering, but they didn't give us any.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Didn't share.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: I mean-- I get-- talk about the officers, I got-- I don't have much use for them. I remember one time I was up at Manhattan Beach, there was three-- three fellows standing on a corner talking. This is a company street. I was walking down the street this kid sitting on the steps said what's it take to make you salute? And I says why, I says you just walked by three officers-- three--three admirals. Says hell, I thought they played in the band. I didn't-- I didn't know there were officers. {cough}

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Thought it was a marching band?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Looked like the Masonic Band. Coming to Cleveland to circus-- they got out of a circus. I didn't know what an officer was. I never seen any officers.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Aside from the officers, did you enjoy the-- the life at sea?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Well, I liked being at sea. I had no problem with that, I like being on boats-- always around the water but I just-- it's just the way that they, like I said there was no food, none of the-- we even had water hours, you know what that is?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What's that again?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Water hours. You know what water hours--

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: You could only wash your hands at a certain time of the day.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: You-- yeah-- you-- because you had to make the water. The best thing they pump the water all forward under the peak tanks, up where I slept and that floor was so hot you couldn't put your feet on it-- your bare feet-- from the-- from the water. And they wouldn't pump it back half because of the ammunition lockers. And I come out of that and I was sleeping up on the-- so I used to go up a deck and sleep in a hammock. And I lay up-- I'd be laying underwater when I wake up. And I had a-- a ____ cover-- like a little tent-- and the damn thing'd leak. And out there it rains all the time. You got two seasons rainy and typhoon season. And it rained you'd actually go through a storm you think it's the end of the world coming but five minutes later bang the decks are steaming and the sun's out. So that's the way-- and I got-- I'm loaded with arthritis. Just from that-- I got a disability pension. So, had a hell of a time getting that. I had to get it through a guy in American Legion. Because they wouldn't do nothing for me. Last time I had an operation they had a-- I had a spinal and I was lying on the operating table and got-- sitting over-- and he hit me three times the back-- you got so damn bad-- your arthritis-- I can't get the needle in.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: This ship had no portholes. Had no places out-- nothing like it is now. No-- we didn't have air-condition-- didn't have no portholes, you had-- I'd go down my bunk and I had a little fan on the wall I'd turn that fan on me go to sleep. The next time I wake up some-- somebody else put it on his bunk. That's-- that's what we had. And no food-- my tonsils were killing me. I wanted to go get an-- a tonsillectomy when we were in the states I couldn't get off because they-- it was 14 days in the hospital for tonsils.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: 14 days.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You have any close buddies or really close--

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I have Andy Stevanic in Sharon, PA. There's him, Wayne (flutes) got a farm down here in _____, Ohio. _____ up there in Michigan and Donald Petersen in Racine, Wisconsin. Yeah, we keep in touch. They're all good kids. _____+ in Florida. They all done in good, too.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When you're onboard ship what kinds of things would you talk about when you were shooting the bull?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Oh, not much of anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Just whatever.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Yeah, talking just-- we were all in our 20's, you know. And we used to catch shark. And-- here, I'll show you some of these pictures.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Catch shark, huh?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Here's the I and R-- I was on this one, that's the Corvus. I was nine months on that light house.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What'd you do to pass the time when you were on that lighthouse?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Played Pinochle, not-- 300 Pinochle and I haven't played cards since.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Got your fill of it?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Oh, God every night. One night I-- here's the-- here's the depth charge racks. This is over at Africa. This is going through the-- this is the life boat we had. Yeah, and one night we got in the-- well, one I night forgot to turn the light on. Forgot who the hell was on watch. Then, the last game we had the keeper got mad and threw everything into the sea and that was the end of the game. He threw the picnic-- the table across the room. There was three of us out there. This is the-- there's a shark.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Okay, is that the _____ certificate for crossing the equator?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: No, this is the International Dateline.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you have to go through that ceremony with--

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: No, I went-- no, we didn't cross the equator.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Coast Guard didn't do that? Yeah--

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: We didn't cross the equator. We didn't cross the equator.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Oh, you didn't cross it, okay.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Here's the (?el paso?). This is the ship that was given up for lost and this is me right here. This is the ship that was overdue five days. Oh, no we didn't cross the equator. We crossed the International Dateline. Here's a picture of the sharks.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Was that good--good eating?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: The small ones are. The officers-- I wished I knew now about saltwater fish-- God almighty stand up there and bow at night we'd see thousands of fish shoot out. Yellowtails-- but I didn't know anything about saltwater fishing-- that I do now. But I wished-- we had nothing to use anyhow. The-- what the-- the fish-- here's the history of the ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So it was the USS Racine?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Named after Racine, Wisconsin.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: That was built right down here at Cleveland Stadium.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What's PF? Patrol--

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Patrol Frigate.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: -- frigate, okay.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: They built-- I think there was-- there was 75 of them and they were all-- all had Navy ships but had Coast Guard crews on them.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Here's all the officers.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Oh, then another time I-- this is the officers-- this is over in Africa-- I had opened up a valve of fire over the-- the diamond plate you know the-- when they're dirty and I cracked this finger right here. Well, I had a ring on. They cut the ring off and I got an infection and this hand began to swell up. And I went to sick bay and the _____+ told me to go down and lay down and you're bunk and put me on the medical list. And they'd have to stand and watch. They give me a hot water bottle. I'm lying down there and this thing's getting bigger and bigger and bigger. Crawling up my arm, it was just swelling. So in the morning I got up about four o'clock and went to the galley to get some hot water. One of the kids in there says the hell's the matter with you? And I showed him and he says Jesus Christ. Come on with me. Why don't we knock down the-- on the doctor's door. The-- was knocking on there-- the doctor looked like-- get down to sick bay. He took me down there, called up the-- called up the executive officer he come down and stood there with me and they gave me a shot of Morphine. And he lanced that. Holy Christ the puss just come out of there. And this-- the ____-- I'll never forget that. So-- and the next day I was laying in my bunk he come down and give me hell for going over his head and-- that was just before we were going on to combat in New York. We pulled out--pulled out of New York-- he had-- he deserted. He jumped ship and left his-- nothing in his locker but a pair of Dungarees. He jumped ship. ____+ kill that guy. Here's the picture of the ship. This is going through the canal here. This is the ____ to ____. Boy you get stiffer than a billy goat on that. Well, that's about it I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during the war, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Yeah. One that scared the hell out of me. I was up-- come off watch-- I was up on watch-- you know on the boat we had to come down three decks-- you go up and iron ladder-- come up I had two buckets of slop, I took it with a rope. And it was about three o'clock in the morning. I had to go through what they called a blackout curtain it's like a big shower curtain. They're black and-- open them up and open up the door to walk out on that deck with two buckets of slop. The next thing I know I'm standing ____+ water right up to here. Jesus Christ. I dropped them buckets and went back into that-- into the-- into the side there. The ship was like this, you know. She had a little fantail. Here. She had a little fantail. And this-- the water-- I was up to my waist in that water. See how it low it is here, back here?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Well, I was up to my waist so I dropped the damn buckets. And then another night I come down on watch-- I went out-- got on my watch and midnight. Come off-- I'd been drinking. And the first thing you do you go down the board, you got to clean the strainers. You got two strainers. Like this-- there's a-- a nut you've got to turn and it's got a cross on it. And it points to which one is live and which one is dead. Well, I'm half stiff and I opened up the wrong one. I looked at oil-- got little specks of oil on my t-shirt. I thought Jesus I'm on the live one. If I'd opened the son of a gun up I would have-- I'd of caught-- blowed the damn ship up.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: That scared the hell out of me. {cough} Yeah, that's about-- and then-- for a while I was the only guy in the ship knew how-- where the held the steam valve was that opened up-- turn the steam out the ____.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Was there any kind of adjustment being there in the-- in the service with guys from all over the country because obviously back then you didn't get much exposure to other people.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: To what-- what do you mean-- other people?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Other people from the South--

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: The guys I didn't like where the-- some of these guys from Texas.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: One time they'd-- this cat was a redneck, too. He was from Georgia. He was a real redneck. And one time they brought a bunch of replacements on, about four or five guys. I looked down there-- standing on the deck I see a colored kid down there. He was-- he was a ____. He had one stripe, you know. And I see him on there. Goddamn it an hour later he was gone. They didn't-- the captain wasn't ready-- he wouldn't have him on his ship. They got rid of him. But I was glad. Because those-- those Goddamn idiots from Texas, they would have thrown him over the side. Those guys were all nuts. You know, it was about four or five of them. They live in a world all their own. We didn't have much social-- didn't hang around-- these seaman never did amount to anything. We never hung around with them. Because-- {cough}-- like I says there's a lot of class restriction on the ship. The black gang sticks with their own group, deck hands with their own. They don't-- you don't do much socializing. Go out drinking-- I think you go out-- you go out with your own group. The only ones I've ever really hung out around were the cooks. When I went in the service my dad says there's two things you want to do. Always make friends with the cooks and don't volunteer for anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: And did you remember that?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Damn right I did. Damn right I did. He was in-- he was in-- over in France and Germany. This guy here-- came and talked with him-- Bobby Briggs. He-- he got a lobster place up in Cape Cod, Maine. And this is the stuff he sends me. Stay in touch with him. And these are guys at the reunion. Wasn't-- only about six or seven of us show up because most of them are all gone. They're just not around anymore.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Well, that's about it I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: What else is there? That's it. Yeah, there was a lot these officers, you know, you had-- you had the academy man and you had the Mustang and you had the 90 day wonders. They--all three-- that was a whole different bunch, too, you know. The captain-- our captain was a-- I say an academy man the rest-- most were 90 day wonders. We had one Mustang, an engineering officer. A real nice fellow. He used to come down the back-- we used to-- our crew always stuck around the back around the fantail. He come down and visit with us-- the captain said if you want to stick with these guys I'll bust you down so you can stay with them. That's the kind of a captain we had.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Woah.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: He didn't want to-- he didn't want to socialize with us. It had no armor on there-- there was nothing else.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: It's what they call a three year hull. This will last you three years, that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: It was just built to last three years, huh?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Just the three years, yeah. Three year hull.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: That's interesting. _____...(2 seconds)

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: That's a joke.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Information about your--

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Highest rank. I was up for-- I was up for Water Tendered First and Goddamn I didn't get it because the Engineering Officer come to me, he says I've got to give it to Joe Chris because he's the regular, you're going home. So I got screwed out of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: I think I've got a pen if you don't.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Here's a pen here.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: All right, great.

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: I got screwed out of another advancement rate. I worked seven days a week. Seven on-- four out of eight off. Seven days a week I made 100 bucks a month. And I was a Second Class Petty Officer.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So no desire to reenlist when your hitch was up, right?

sp.speaker: Robert J. Turner
sp.p: Well, I could have-- they would have give me an advancement rating and then they had that they were going to drop that bomb on _____+. And they had-- on the Boulevard to swing over. You go onto that you know-- you get an advancement rating. But I-- the hell with it, I want to get home. By that time I'd had enough. I even got sick of wearing the same damn uniforms all the time. You get-- you never-- no colors, you know. You just-- you just don't want to do it. I took the damn uniform off, I never put it on. That was it.
